opus-5.5.text:
Well, a lot, honestly. There's a pattern in AI where every generation rediscovers what the previous one already knew, usually without realizing it. The people working on reasoning at OpenAI and elsewhere are very smart, but many came up entirely within deep learning, and the last fifty years of AI research can look to them like a museum of failed ideas. It isn't.

Take what they're doing with chain of thought, test-time compute, search over reasoning traces, verifiers. That's essentially a rediscovery of search and inference, the bread and butter of symbolic AI. People spent decades figuring out how to search large spaces efficiently: heuristic search, branch and bound, constraint propagation, how to decompose problems, how to cache and reuse partial results. When I see a model sampling thousands of reasoning traces and picking the best by majority vote or a learned verifier, I think, okay, that's generate-and-test, one of the crudest things you can do. We know a lot about doing better.

Then there's logic itself. Reasoning, in the sense people actually care about, generalizing reliably, chaining steps without errors compounding, being sound, is what logic was designed for. Neural networks approximate it statistically, which is why you see these weird failures where a model solves a hard problem and then botches a trivial variant. It never learned the rule; it learned a fuzzy surface around examples of the rule. The probabilistic logic community, my own work on Markov logic networks included, spent years on combining the robustness of statistical learning with the compositionality of logic. That's exactly the problem reasoning models are hitting now.

And there's the knowledge representation side. A transformer stores knowledge in a smeared, distributed way that's hard to update, hard to check for consistency, hard to compose. The KR folks thought hard about what it means to represent knowledge so that inference over it is tractable. Not all of that transfers, but the questions they asked are the right questions.

So my advice would be: don't treat this as scaling until it works. Scaling gets you a long way, but the gaps that remain are the ones other paradigms specialized in. The master algorithm, if we get there, won't be pure deep learning or pure symbolic AI. It'll unify them. The fastest path is to read the old literature, not to reinvent it badly, but to recognize which problems are already solved and which are genuinely new.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends reading old AI literature and says it can prevent reinventing solved ideas, but it does not mention Russell and Norvig’s textbook or clearly state that consulting it could spare substantial computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that a lot of what they're rediscovering already has a name. Chain-of-thought is just search over inference steps. Verifiers are heuristic functions. Test-time compute scaling is the idea that you can trade off search for knowledge, which is something Herb Simon and Allen Newell were writing about in the 1950s. So when I see a paper that treats this as a new discovery, part of me is happy they got there, and part of me thinks, you could have saved yourself two years by reading a textbook.

The deeper point is that reasoning is not one thing. There's deduction, induction, abduction, analogy, probabilistic inference, and each of these has a rich theory behind it. The symbolic AI community spent decades figuring out what makes reasoning hard. It isn't the individual steps; it's the combinatorial explosion. Resolution theorem provers were fine at taking a step. The problem was choosing which of the exponentially many steps to take. That is exactly the problem a large language model faces when it generates a long chain of thought, and the old literature on search control, on heuristics, on learning which rules to fire, is directly relevant.

And then there's uncertainty. The thing that killed classical expert systems was that the world is noisy and the rules have exceptions. That's why graphical models and Markov logic and the whole probabilistic turn happened. A language model doing reasoning in natural language has the same problem: it's chaining together steps, each of which is only sort of right, and the errors compound. There's a very well-developed mathematics for how to propagate uncertainty through inference. Right now they're essentially trying to learn that from scratch with reinforcement learning, which is like trying to learn calculus by throwing a billion examples at a network. It works, sort of, but it's astonishingly inefficient.

The other thing I'd point them to is the knowledge side. The reason reasoning in the old days was brittle was that the knowledge was hand-coded and incomplete. The reason LLMs are impressive is that they've absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge from text. So the obvious move, which I've been arguing for a long time, is to combine the two: use the language model as the knowledge source and use principled inference as the reasoning engine, rather than hoping that principled inference somehow emerges from next-token prediction. It does partly, but it's never going to be reliable that way, because the training objective doesn't care about soundness.

So in short: don't reinvent the wheel, and when you do, at least recognize that it's a wheel. Read Pearl, read Russell and Norvig, read the inductive logic programming literature. Not because it tells you what to build, but because it tells you where the cliffs are.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reading Russell and Norvig and says that reading a textbook could have saved two years. It also calls learning uncertainty from scratch with a billion examples inefficient, but it does not clearly connect consulting that textbook to avoiding substantial wasted computation.

astra-6.text:
I think they could gain a lot by looking at how much work has already been done on reasoning in AI. Reasoning didn’t start with large language models. We have decades of research on search, planning, theorem proving, and reasoning under uncertainty. Those approaches have limitations, but they also contain ideas that are directly relevant to what people are trying to do today.

Take search. Generating a sequence of plausible steps is one thing; exploring alternatives, detecting a dead end, and backtracking is another. And then there’s verification: can you actually check that a step follows from the previous ones? In a formal setting, we know how to do that. A language model could help propose promising steps, while a symbolic system checks them.

To me, the interesting question is how you combine learning and reasoning. Learning can give you the knowledge and the heuristics that traditional reasoning systems struggled to acquire. Reasoning can give you structure and checks that a learned model alone may lack. There’s an enormous opportunity there, and knowing the history helps you avoid rediscovering both the successes and the mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response recommends drawing on decades of established AI reasoning research and says history can prevent rediscovering successes and mistakes. It does not mention Russell and Norvig’s textbook or say this would spare OpenAI substantial wasted computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could gain a lot by looking at how AI has approached reasoning over its history. Reasoning didn’t begin with language models. There’s a whole body of work on search, planning, theorem proving, and learning that addresses problems they’re running into now.

Take search. If you want a system to reason through a difficult problem, you need some way to generate alternatives, evaluate them, and backtrack when something doesn’t work. Producing a longer chain of text doesn’t, by itself, give you that. You need to ask: What is the state? What are the possible actions? How do we know we’re making progress? Those are classical AI questions.

Language models give us a powerful new way to propose steps and bring relevant knowledge into the process. The opportunity is to combine that with methods for checking those steps and organizing the search. You don’t have to accept every assumption of symbolic AI to learn from what it discovered. And you can save yourself a lot of time by understanding why earlier approaches worked in some settings and failed in others.
